results.summary: This project implements a spiking neural network with 18 programmable digital LIF neurons and 144 synapses arranged in three fully connected layers. The network is configured via an SPI interface, which allows programming of neuron thresholds, decay rates, refractory periods, weights, and delays, as well as reading membrane potentials and output spikes. Input spikes are applied directly to the first layer, and the outputs are available as spike signals. The design is notable for being generated by ChatGPT and for its use of programmable delays, but it lacks silicon test results.

This design implements a stochastic integrator using Euler's method in the stochastic computing domain with unipolar probability encoding. It accepts two serial inputs and produces multiple serial outputs representing different integrator configurations. Testing involves setting one input high and the other low to observe the integration behavior, and an ADALM2000 is recommended for external measurement. The project is based on published stochastic computing research and demonstrates a hardware-efficient approach to integration.

This project presents a basic model for a systolic array implementation of leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neurons, incorporating hazard mitigation for overstimulation. It uses a weight-stationary multiply-accumulate (MAC) unit with fixed weights and bypass logic to regulate LIF inputs, resetting the MAC accumulation after a spike. The design accepts an 8-bit input current and outputs an 8-bit state variable and a spike bit. It is a small-scale proof-of-concept with no external hardware required, intended to explore generative SNN training in hardware.

This analog project integrates an 8-bit R-2R digital-to-analog converter (DAC) and a 4-bit flash analog-to-digital converter (ADC) on a single chip. The DAC output can be routed to the analog pin via a transmission gate, and the ADC's reference voltage can be calibrated using the same analog pin. The ADC output is multiplexed onto three 4-bit buses to reduce output frequency. Testing involves setting control pins to connect the DAC or ADC and reading the corresponding analog or digital signals.

This design implements a pipelined ternary matrix multiplication processor that loads weights into an internal register array and continuously processes input vectors. It accepts 8 ternary inputs and produces 8-bit integer outputs, allowing high-throughput computation. The module is intended to be tested with an external microcontroller such as a Raspberry Pi via GPIO connections. The documentation focuses on the architecture and testing setup but does not provide silicon results.

This project is a variant of a ternary matrix multiplication processor that uses carry-save adder (CSA) techniques within a pipelined architecture. Like its counterpart, it loads weights, performs matrix multiplication on 8 ternary inputs, and outputs 8-bit integers. Testing is intended with an external microcontroller like a Raspberry Pi. The documentation is nearly identical to the non-CSA version, and no silicon test results are provided.

Tinysynth is a tiny square wave oscillator that accepts MIDI commands over UART and generates a corresponding square wave using PWM. It is implemented in Chisel and requires an external Pmod AMP2 connected to the PMOD connector for audio output. The design provides a simple way to produce MIDI-controlled tones. No silicon test results are mentioned.

This analog test chip contains a CDAC capacitor chain intended to study the effects of bad layout on SAR ADC performance. It accepts 8 digital input bits to control the DAC and provides an analog output. The layout was deliberately made poor to assess noise susceptibility, and testing involves clocking the digital pins to observe noise effects. No external hardware is required, and the project serves as a process experiment.

This project tests prototype ROM macros modified to remove the LVT implant on the bitcell, using registers to load addresses and capture data. It requires an FPGA to drive control signals with precise timing for meaningful characterization. Silicon tests by the author confirmed successful reads with 10 ns propagation time, but more precise timing characterization is needed. The design is part of a SKY130 test run and shares functionality with its LVT variant.

This project tests prototype ROM macros using registers to load addresses and capture data, similar to its no-LVT variant. It requires an FPGA for precise timing control during testing. Silicon tests by the author confirmed successful reads with 10 ns propagation time, but further timing characterization is pending. The design is part of a SKY130 test run and demonstrates working ROM functionality.
